This game is polarizing and I understand because it can be a great game but also extremely frustrating also.

Things I like:
- the story seems interesting
- the fighting mechanics and animations are really good
- some of the graphics look stunning especially for a free game
- the genre of being a mixed rpg/mmo/open-world/mixed bag is interesting
- it's free and all this amount of content for free is really amazing

Things I don't like:
- the story is hard to follow lol imo, it's hard to track your quests because they have packed so much content into it and there's not a linear thread of what to do next with all the content whereas other games like FFXIV, it's clear to know where to go next
- the massive amount of content and things that are flashing/trying to get your attention can be distracting and disorienting
- sometimes the graphics are really doodoo
- the UI is REALLY REALLY hard to navigate, it's a lot of self-learn and unintuitive
- the game sounds pretty bad in English; the tone/pacing is kinda weird at times

Overall i'd give it a 6.8/10there's a lot to like and a LOT to improve - and the studio definitely can improve but we'll see. I'd recommend people to try it to get their own opinion as well.

Playing Where Winds Meet honestly surprised me in the best way. From the moment I stepped into its version of ancient China, I felt like I was actually exploring a living world instead of just following markers on a map. The landscapes are stunning—wide open fields, quiet villages, misty mountains—and every place I visited made me want to keep going just to see what was next.

What hooked me the most was the combat. It’s fast, fluid, and really makes you feel like a true wuxia hero. Dodging, countering, jumping off rooftops, chaining abilities—everything flows so well that even regular fights feel cinematic. It’s the kind of combat system that makes you want to fight just because it feels good.

The story pulled me in too. It gives you freedom to play things your own way while still offering characters and quests that feel meaningful. Even the smaller side missions are interesting and add to the world instead of feeling like filler.

Yeah, there are a few rough edges here and there, but nothing that took away from my experience. Overall, Where Winds Meet gave me that rare feeling of actually being on an adventure—not just playing a game.

If you love open-world games, martial-arts combat, or just exploring beautiful environments, I’d definitely recommend giving it a try.

I've never played a free-to-play game before because I always knew I wouldn't enjoy them because of PTW aspects. I've always hated the un-immersive nature and slimy tactics they seem to use to get you to spend money in game.
So this is technically my first because I heard it isn't PTW, and I have to say, I'm very glad I did. I'm having a great time and my character and the outfit I have are very appealing. I don't feel the need to spend any money in game.
I'm sure there are ways you can pay for convenience, but so far I haven't felt annoyed at the pace of the game, or that I was being handicapped or held back in any way by not spending money.
This is how free-to-play games should be. 
As of now, I still don't intend to spend any money because I'm kinda cheap, but at the same time, I hope there are plenty of people supporting the game, because in my opinion it certainly deserves it.

But the game is great overall. China knows what's up, that's for sure. Is this game for real? I'm genuinely shocked at how good this game is and how not a scam it is. It sucks that it's come to that, but I gotta give this dev their flowers. It's very obvious that a lot of attention to detail and actual care and respect for the players was put into this game and that's all we freaking ask for. Kind of ironic I'd gladly pay for this game if I could, and eventually, I will probably buy something cosmetic because that's what actual good games do to you lol.

This is a very good approach to the gacha genre. The realistic graphics, all the good mechanics you get and think "Hey, this is cool, I have definitely seen this in another game".

The problems many players see, including myself, are the endless menus and the bloated UI.

I do not quite know why this is a thing in this type of games. My best guess is that the whole menus-UI setup is a filler, because, oh boy, is it time consuming!

Also, I would like to point out how incredibly weak the stealth system is. I feel like they missed a great opportunity there.

Overall, it is a free game (obviously the income comes from the microtransactions), the theme is great, the graphics are great, the story and the side quests are good, but it can be made even better.

I just hope they solve all these annoying traditional gacha aspects someday. It is dragging the whole thing down like crazy.

A suggestion: Instead of having to press a specific button hidden deep beneath the menus, and then do the same thing for 20 buttons, im order to get your rewards, just have a "Claim all" button.

In case it is indeed a filler feature, I don't think you have to worry about slowing down the player, the game is massive.

Where Winds Meet is a beautifully crafted wuxia open-world RPG that mixes cinematic martial arts, exploration, and absolute chaos in the best way possible.

My first half hour vanished inside character customization, and the second half hour disappeared while I tried naming my hero. I tested more than fifty names, every single one was taken, and in the end I had to add a prefix just to start my journey. For my second hour, I spent most of it dying repeatedly to the Puppeteer’s spear. And somehow, the next five hours slipped away as I wandered through the beautiful wuxia world, completely absorbed by its landscapes and atmosphere.
The game is fully free-to-play and monetized only through cosmetics and battle passes—no pay-to-win, no predatory gacha. Performance can vary, and the menu system is so complicated it feels like the real final boss, but once you understand it, everything flows.

Combat is “Souls-light,” rewarding good timing without punishing you too hard. The world is packed with bosses, puzzles, treasures, side quests, and a surprisingly deep social system—raids, PvP, sects and more (I have to explore that). You also get odd but heroic jobs, like removing someone’s itchy back, immobilizing a molester, or healing ducks… though never fight the ducks. They are secretly boss-level enemies. And Elder Gongsun—please, Let me hit You. And there is some Shaming Prisoner Activity with Special Time Limit.

Overall, Where Winds Meet is a stylish, chaotic, and surprisingly heartwarming wuxia adventure. Between the stunning open world, flexible playstyles, cinematic combat, and the absurd stories it creates, it’s easily one of the most memorable free RPG experiences available.

Where Winds Meet implements both tried and true mechanics while also exploring new ideas. 

It took me a while to like the title as I am not a fan of Wuxia films. The flying combat and 1 vs 1000 style of martial arts films don’t really appeal to me, yet they work really well for a video game. Couple that with a high combat difficulty (when playing on harder modes) and you can get a lot of enjoyment from this title.

If combat does not appeal to you, there are other MMO lifeskill-like elements to this game that might pique your interest. For example, you can make friends with a lot of NPC’s. Not all of them, but a fair number of them. To do this requires getting on their good side. How? Through an AI chat bot. Yes, you have to befriend NPC’s by chatting with them and encouraging them to do certain things. Each one is unique and can only discuss what they know. They are not ‘all knowing’ as most modern AI chatbots can be.

If you have a craving for a good MMO, this could be it. You can switch between solo mode and online mode which displays dozens of players at a time in the world. Each mode has their pros and cons and if you want the full experience, you’ll have to play through both modes. 

The only other game I can think of that does something similar is Elite: Dangerous. I’m glad the feature is picking up.

All in all, this game gets a 10/10 - it’s a solid MMO that tries a lot of new things (too much to list), so I suggest you give it a shot. It is free, after all.

“A Beautiful Chaos of Kung-Fu, Myth… and Bear-Throwing” — ★★★★☆ (9/10)

Where Winds Meet is an absolute blast — a gorgeous, chaotic wuxia playground where every cliff, village, and battlefield feels alive. The combat is fast, flashy, and packed with style, and the world begs you to explore every inch of it. But let’s be honest: none of that compares to the game’s greatest achievement…

You can throw a bear.

Yes. A full-sized, roaring, fur-covered beast — launched into the air by the sheer power of martial arts. That alone is worth at least 9 stars.

So why only a 9/10 and not a perfect score?

Because for some reason… you can’t throw wolves.
How do you let me grab a bear by the scruff and yeet it into the horizon but deny me the joy of wolf-launching? It's a tragedy of game design.

And while we’re on the topic…

Let me throw the bosses.

If I can hurl a bear into orbit, why can’t I pick up a towering armored warlord and send him flying with peak wuxia energy? The game’s already wild — just go all the way. Give me boss-yeeting.

Final Verdict:

9/10 — A spectacular, stylish wuxia adventure filled with freedom, flair, and unforgettable moments. Add wolf-throwing, boss-throwing, and it’s an easy 10/10 legend.

Important Survival Tip:

Do NOT fight the goose.
He is a martial god. You are but a wandering mortal. Respect him and walk away.

WWM delivers a captivating, visually stunning open-world martial arts epic that feels less like a game and more like a journey through a living painting. Wherever you set foot, you’re met with an immersive scene that begs to be admired, making exploration not just a pastime, but a genuine pleasure.
The open world is rich with possibilities. You’re free to pursue what you enjoy most: engage in challenging combats (either PvE or PvP), or simply lose yourself in leisure activities.
Performance is another strong suit. The game is well optimized, running smoothly even on modest PC setups without sacrificing visual fidelity. 

That said, the game isn’t without its flaws. The menu interface presents a significant learning for beginners, with layered UI that can feel unintuitive at first. Furthermore, some boss fights suffer from awkward camera angles that can frustrate rather than challenge, for example: can't see shjt whenever the bosses jump up and land hit. Another downside is the bad netcode in PvP, where intermittent lag and latency issues can disrupt the precise timing required for competitive combat. Funny that I even had one player directly messaged me after a PvP match telling me to fix my ping whereas the issue is not on my end. Still, the game is incredibly good for a F2P title.

*Note for challenge seekers: start the game on Legend mode, it is fun. You can't switch to Legend once you choose to play on lower difficulty, don't know if devs are working on fixing this.

You can buy costumes for your character, if you like, and they run from reasonably cheap to very expensive- but they are simply skins and don't change the game by adding power etc. Be aware that there are also 'free' costumes you can find, and earn through questing, etc., in the game and they are absolutely cool too. My only hang up, at the beginning when the game launched, was feeling overwhelmed by the amount of content and information being tossed at me…I felt like I couldn’t keep up with the menus (clunky, but the devs are working on that issue) and I'm one of those player types who likes to 'do'—teach me, let me actually practice for a bit to start some muscle memory, then throw me in the deep end lol. That and the terrain sometimes grabbing my character are my only gripes.

The various ways you can play Where Winds Meet is really interesting. Currently I'm playing the game solo, like a single player RPG. But I can easily group up with r/l friends who are playing for co-op. I could play it like an MMO too if I choose. I love the fact I have choice and am not being forced to play any particular way.

The questing (main, side) are actually interesting, not filled with agenda white noise, and many of them are actually fun to progress. I've yet to run into something I consider tedious. I also don't find the game grindy and I've played some grinders in the past (Lineage II anyone?). Getting materials to upgrade gear slots isn't difficult—the menu will tell you what you need and can show you the ways to obtain it, and even mark your map for you.

There is a crafting system that seems to work smoothly but I haven't spent much time with it, other than to make some potions and cook some meals.

Where Winds Meet is vast game. There is a lot to take in, a lot to learn, for sure. The best part is, this game really brings Wuxia and the Jiang hu world to life. Well worth the time. YMMV.

[h1]One of the most ambitious games I've ever played[/h1]
Where Winds Meet is a wild game. I don't think I've ever seen a game where you can roleplay as a villain and go around killing NPCs, have bounties placed on you, get hunted by other players, get jailed if you get caught, and then to cut your sentence short, get paraded around town while other players hurl cabbages and eggs at you.
Oh, and this game also has raids, pvp, and a whole ass battle royale system built into it. This game tries to do a bit of everything and amazingly, it kinda pulls it off!

There's enough content packed into this one game that anyone should be able to find something they like. Don't want to fight? Just explore, take screenshots, play musical instruments (players have figured out Linkin Park on the Guzheng), heal NPCs or other players, dance, wrestle, play chess, quiz, wrestle... the list goes on. 
Want hardcore fights? Fight challenging bosses solo or co-op, take out enemy camps head on or stealthily, tune your gear, experiment with different builds, join raids etc...

You get the idea. There is a ridiculpus number of things you can do in this game. And it's all [b]free[/b], so what is there to lose by giving it a try?

Where Winds Meet isn’t a game — it’s a social experiment to see how fast you’ll question your intelligence. You load in thinking you’re a wuxia legend, but the game immediately clocks your skill level and goes,
“Ah yes… a disappointment has arrived.”
You think you’re a wuxia prodigy? Cute. The game takes one look at your button-mashing and says, “aw… adorable… now perish.”

Story? Honestly… I’m still not sure. NPCs talk like they’re dropping ancient wisdom, but half the time I’m too busy chasing butterflies or trying not to fall off cliffs. Priorities, right?

Parkour? Chef’s kiss. The climbing system makes you feel like Spider-Man got reincarnated as a martial artist. You will fall. You will scream. You will climb again. Growth mindset.

Performance? Depends. Some days it runs like a smooth kung-fu movie. Other days it feels like your GPU is writing its resignation letter.

Everything kills you.
Everything.
Even your own decisions.

Animals? They hate you.
Bandits? They mock you.
Gravity? It has a personal vendetta.

At this point, you’re not playing the game.
You’re performing cosmic slapstick for the universe’s amusement.

50/10 — your dignity will not survive, but at least the scenery is nice.

[b]Gameplay[/b]
Combat:
For a free-to-play game, the combat system is surprisingly decent, but it doesn’t come close to the depth or challenge of something like Elden Ring. Most boss fights can be beaten by simply standing your ground, timing attacks, and parrying without needing much movement or strategy. I haven’t tried the harder difficulties yet, so maybe they improve the experience, but I personally wish the game had a single fixed difficulty setting (with the exception of a dedicated hardcore mode).

Stealth, puzzles, and side activities:
The game really shines in its variety of side content. Stealth missions, puzzles, and other unique activities are creative and fun, adding a lot more playable hours and making the world feel more alive.

[b]Story[/b]
Side dialogues:
These are often dull and filled with unnecessary lines that don’t add to the lore or the main narrative. The worst part is when the game uses dialogue just to explain gameplay mechanics—there should be simpler, cleaner ways to teach the player without forcing them to read through long, pointless conversations.

Main story:
It can be hard to follow, mainly because the excessive dialogue makes it confusing to figure out what’s actually important. The story lacks strong character development, and many plot points feel predictable.

[b]Interface (UI/UX)[/b]
The interface is overwhelming when you first start. It’s cluttered with too many menus, tabs, and features that could easily be grouped together. All players really need is a clean inventory tab and a simple skill section. I want to play the game—not spend hours digging through menus.

[b]Graphics & Environment[/b]
This is one of the game’s strongest points. The visual quality is very good, and the world is huge and detailed. It’s genuinely impressive that a free-to-play game can deliver such a massive and visually appealing environment.

A game I expected to be absolute slop but is actually a ton of fun, it's F2P and blows a ton of paid AAA titles out of the water. I had to admittedly rough out some areas, and get accustomed to some of the games quirks. It took me a few hours till the game clicked once it did it got its hooks into me. Note I'm reviewing this game on the basis of playing on "Legend" difficulty.

Pros
- Satisfying parry centric gameplay that provides a nice challenge. Difficulty options and parry assists are available for players if you want.
- Varied dungeon mechanics, bosses
- Challenging
- Not P2W with the cash shop being for glamour
- Lovely visuals, setting and some nice storylines.
- Multiple progression points with a surprising emphasis on horizontal progression (I prefer horizontal over vertical).
- The map is well populated with something to do or find that helps with overall progression.
- Various activities to do that give stat gains/desirable rewards. Chinese Chess, Drunk Darts, Fishing, Playing Music, Archery Contests, Drinking Contests, Sumo, Mahjong, Cards, Dancing.
- Faction system with various rules and playstyles to progress in.
- Lots of player build customization with varied playstyles. Sword, Large Swords, Dual Blades, Spears, Fans, Umbrellas, Rope Dart, some weapons having multiple styles that change their playstyle.
- Tons of player freedom after scripted opening.
- Shared open world co-op. Up to you and 4 other players only limitation being story quests are NOT co-op capable.
- The game is well optimized with me being able to maintain a constant 120fps.

Cons
- Inexcusable UI that needs to be reworked. This is easily the worst part of this game and if the game wasn't so damn fun I would have quit because of it.

- Controller navigation in some mini games and menus is questionable to the point that I use my mouse instead.

- Horrible player onloading, the game dumps you in after the intro and quickly starts to pile on elements often without giving the player any context other than that a thing exists. It makes it difficult especially early on to discern if something is important or not and where to focus. This specific issue is made worse with the game having various currencies, early on it's hard to know what does what and how to earn each one. (I don't have an issue with multiple currencies but it took a while to hash out what was what).

- Gear progression trappings. When you uncap levels the game provides a starter set of gear to onload you to that level range as the game world syncs to your uncaps. This puts it into the players head that they just equip this set and forget because early on this is perfectly fine, but falling into this habit is a mistake. For example when I uncapped to level 50, my prior level range set was much better than the provided because the set bonus synergy to my kit along with the bonus effects I rolled on the pieces. The game makes it easy to fall into equip X item because highest number, and you see many players doing it because of this. Because of this players slap on equipment without thinking about the set effects, stat rolls, etc. which can make you get one shotted or have horrid damage output. One could blame the player for not critically thinking about this scenario but honestly the developers instill this mentality into the players head from their design so I'd fault them for it over the player.

- Cases of bad translation and untranslated text.

Your mileage may vary aspects
- Progression style. If you prefer vertical progression this game has aspects that could be a dealbreaker for you. The are time gates on level uncaps (You still gain exp it's stored for the next uncap) which eventually roll into taking days before you can uncap, a stamina system which takes about 3 IRL days to fully recharge (You can use any accumulated stamina at any time along with stamina regen items if you have any.) for getting rewards from multiplayer boss fights, raids, etc. You don't run out of things to do because of these limiters despite what others may state as the game gives various stats, passives, skills and what not from doing the open world content not leveling/stamina activities. With this being a large part of the game if you dislike doing various types of content and only like leveling this will likely be an issue.

- AI chat bot NPCs you can interact with to befriend and earn weekly rewards. Essentially you converse with NPCs that have a certain set personality and scenario you need to resolve for them, once you do this you befriend them and they'll send weekly gifts with the more you befriend the better weekly rewards. Personally I've had some interesting interactions that I think gives some justification to this interaction such as angering the NPC in the chat that they end it and just outright attack me, or using absurd methods to resolve the chat situation. If you're completely anti-AI then I guess this would be the deal breaker.

- Mobage aspects. The game has dailies, weeklies, battle pass (free and paid tracks), multiple currencies, stamina, gatcha for cosmetics, menus designed like a mobage.

After finishing the story (which more content will be added) I loved EVERYTHING. The cinematics, the QTE, The fight styles. I REALLY loved the game. A lot of feels like dark souls and I am really loving it. 

Despite the game is a gacha game, by the looks of it, the game is not competitive. It feels very fair and the game's only gacha is the cosmetics which I adore it. I hope to see a lot more in this game!

If you look at this game and see something that you think you might like, then just try it. It's free, and I can assure you that you will not ever be required to spend money to enjoy what the game has to offer. 

The developers insist that there is no pay2win, and they're not lying. Yes, you can technically get a few consumable items that temporarily buff your stats in a very minor way from the draw shop (the gacha shop), but I never used any of these, and I played on the hardest difficulty (Legend) and beat most of the bosses at the time of writing. I only spent some money because I felt obligated to give back to the devs after all the time I've spent enjoying it for free, plus I got a pretty dress out of it.

Time investment is a slightly different story. There's a lot of mechanics related to character progression that are tied to grinding, whether its grinding upgrade materials, gear, upgrades to "Inner Way" techniques (playstyle-dictating passives), etc. There's a lot to work towards, but that's not necessarily a bad thing for those that like always having something to build up. Even after beating nearly every boss, it still feels like my character is nowhere near at peak power, and I don't know if I'll ever reach total mastery. The grind fits the themes of the game, too, making you truly feel like a student of martial arts that must practice a single punch a thousand times or what have you. 

This is a live-service game, though, so there are things that try to get you to commit time to this game across weeks, if not months. The are some mechanics that arbitrarily limit how much grinding and progress you can achieve in a week (mostly Jade Fish and weekly shop stock). Global level caps keep everyone from leveling up too quickly, forcing you to wait a week or more before being allowed to unlock the next set of levels. Materials for upgrading gear only apply to the specific tier of gear its designed for, making you grind for different materials each time you reach a new level cap. Claiming rewards for doing boss or outpost challenges requires Stamina, which you have a limited amount of, and it can take several days for it to fully regenerate naturally (though, again, you CANNOT pay to skip the wait, which is ultimately a good thing). All these things are meant to get you to come back to this game every so often, even if its for just a couple hours a day. I personally don't love it, but I also don't hate it. It's a good thing for those looking for a game they can fall back on, and it only really matters to those looking to min/max. If you're just looking to enjoy the game casually, then these systems don't really affect you, thankfully.

There are a few other "meh" things about this game that are consequences of the game's business model, but these have less to do with the time/money investment and more to do with the general quality of the experience. 

The game bombards you with menus hidden in menus hidden in menus, and each of these menus is associated with different claimable rewards that you get from doing just about anything. In the early game especially, you'll complete a quest or something and you'll get like 10 different notifications for rewards you can claim, each taking you to a different menu meant to display your progress in one of the game's many systems. It's overwhelming and honestly turned me off from the game the first few days I tried it, but eventually you get used to it, the notifications become less and less frequent, and you'll eventually get a handle on it. I think the reason these menus exist is to guide the player towards the content that has rewards so the player always knows what to do to get what they want. I don't really like this approach, I appreciate when a game keeps things hidden and isn't scared of the player missing content, but whatever, you can ignore most of it.

The other consequence of this game's live-service nature is that it is essentially a perpetual "work in progress." The early parts of the game will feel pretty feature-complete and decently polished, but the further along you go the more incomplete the game will feel. Characters will go from having detailed backstories to having placeholder text for descriptions. You'll walk towards an ominous looking building before the game teleports you away and says the area is still under development. You'll finish the main quest and be told to wait 3 months before you can start the next part of it because they're not done making it yet. If this was a single-purchase game, it would be labelled Early Access. I wish the game was a complete package with a beginning, middle, and end, but that's not the case, and it will likely continue to not be the case for quite some time yet. It makes me look forward to future content updates, but in a sort of bittersweet kind of way.

What I've said up till now has been to give you an overview of the game's free to play model and its consequences so you can set your expectations accordingly. I haven't talked about what I actually like about the game itself yet, and that's honestly because it may not even be relevant to you. There's SO many things to do in this game, that what you get out of it is likely to be very different from what I got out of it. You could spend all your time exploring the world, or spend it hunting bosses, or spend it playing minigames, or spend it taking pictures of the pretty scenery, or spend it doing player bounties, or spend it competing in the arena, or...you get it. The game has a little bit of everything for every type of player, so my only advice to you is to focus on the parts of the game that you personally find enjoyable. For me, that was dungeon crawling, fighting bosses, playing madiao, and spending way too much time in photo mode.

For me, this game was exciting, beautiful, charming, emotional, challenging, and rewarding. It's epic scope and cinematic flair are juxtaposed by somber quiet and a sincere appreciation for the beauty of the natural world and the human spirit. Its AAA grandiosity stands in stark contrast to its goofy little quirks, oddball sense of humor, and its fanboyish commitment to wuxia fantasy. It doesn't nail everything it attempts to do absolutely flawlessly, but I honestly think its daring that they even made such a grand attempt in the first place and provide it for free.

I can only hope that things don't get any worse with future updates. I'm cautiously optimistic, but we'll see.

This is my first ever Steam review. Writing this after 103.9 hours into the game. Let me tell you this, I have not finished the main story quests. I have played video games for 30 years or more and I absolutely love video games. I am a sucker for especially open world game and role playing game as well. This game has it all, it checked all the boxes for the type of game I like.

Okay, enough about my gaming history and let's get to it. First lets talk about the technical stuffs, this game engine is something, it looks beautiful and also stable. I have never experience any crashes or inconsistency in frame rate. I play this game on 2 devices, ASUS G14 2024 RTX 4060 with 32gb and ASUS ROG Ally X. Both runs smoothly, on my Ally X the small screen and put it on Medium with 900p with Frame Generation gets around 55-60 frames per second, if you want more FPS you need to drop it to 720p to get more. I play 1080p on my laptop and connect it to an external monitor, and it is amazing and stable. I am an abomination of a PC gamer, I use controller just to let you know.

In terms of bugs or glitches, I mostly encountered it on the map, especially tracking mob for materials. Other than that, everything else are smooth sailing. The fact that so minimal loading screen even when go to underground or discover dungeons is amazing, the game never tried to pull you away from the game with loading screen (looking at you Starfield).

Let's talk about the experience. On how I play this game, I just explore, run around, collect things, and thanks to playing Death's Stranding I barely do any fast travel, I walk and run. No mount. Exploring and curiousity are rewarded well in this game, I stumbled upon the Qinghe "campaign bosses" mostly by accidents. I explore, found quests explore a dungeon and then BOOM! THere is a boss at the end. I absolutely love it. I get wrecked most of the time, but that is the experience. Talking about getting wrecked by bosses, I play on recommended difficulty. I by no means a person that dabble into souls-borne game. In fact the only souls-borne game I finished was Elden Ring. The difficulty for me is fair, i do rage quit and stop fighting the boss and go do something else. That is the beauty, I can stop doing what I am doing and still enjoy the game. So in short, my experience so far is exploring, stumble upon bosses, dungeons, or quests. I think I need to finish the main story soon but I get distracted very easily. after 103 hours, I am only at 63% in Qinghe exploration. I just barely arrived in Kaifeng. 

So are there any bad things with this game, plenty. I am sure there are plenty of reviews pointing out the herendous UI and menus to keep track of everything. Especially when trying to get that RED NOTIFICATION AND YOU DON'T KNOW WHERE THE REWARDS ARE! Trying to know and upgrade skills and weapon took me almost a week to remember where there are. I am sure in the future if the devs really care about global audience they will fix this, but time will tell.

The gacha? All cosmetics and I have no idea what the rate are. I bought the Battlepass, just to see what is there to offered. I think the devs need to give better rewards after level 50 of the Battlepass. There are controversial decision that the devs made with prices on global version are more expensive than the China version. If you play this game you should voice out this concern, about us the global version players are not treated equally in terms of the pricing. Personally, I would not buy any of the 2k above cosmetics. Each of us choose to spend or not it is up to you.

Speaking of spending money or not, this game is still awesome if you don't buy cosmetic. i randomly finished a quest and it gave me a set of cosmetics! I'm like what? Really?! The cosmetic that was part of the reward from a quest looks good as well. The amount of content for a free-to-play game in this game is epicly HUGE!

Overall, this game is amazing. I love spending time in the world. Run around, explore, help people (I play healer) in the Multiplayer mode. I cannot even imagine the amount of content that are still not released to us yet. This is my main game now. Sacrificed a lot of games just to give space for this. I will keep on playing and hopefully the enthusiasm I have for exploring still burns bright like the Morning Star for time to comes. 

Hopefully this review makes you feel the same way as how I enjoyed the game. If you disagree, well, you are right. This is just my humble opinion. Nothing more, nothing less. Those that are on the fence give it a try. Those still playing and enjoying it, keep playing. This game respect your time, though it have been sucking the sleep out of me. But that is completely my fault. Well that's it, see you in the game.

Where Winds Meet – Feedback So Far

I’m absolutely loving Where Winds Meet so far. The story is fantastic, the visuals are a straight 10/10 and the character models and customization options are some of the best I’ve seen in any game. Weapon designs are incredibly well done and the variety keeps combat interesting. Overall gameplay feels smooth, steady and consistently engaging.

That said, there are a few areas that could make the experience even better:

Energy Costs for Bosses and POIs: The current energy system can feel a bit restrictive. Either reducing the energy required or offering more frequent or accessible ways to earn energy would make exploration and boss encounters flow more naturally.*

Healing in PvP Bounties: Healing feels a little overtuned in PvP bounty fights. Either lowering the effectiveness or adding a mechanic that allows players to interrupt or temporarily disable healing would help keep battles fair and skill-based.*

RNG on Weapon and Armor Rolls: The RNG system can feel punishing. While god rolls shouldn’t be easy, having gear roll poorly 99 out of 100 times makes progression feel more frustrating than rewarding. Slightly improving the balance here would go a long way without removing the challenge.*

Overall, the foundation of the game is amazing and refining these systems would help it reach its full potential. Looking forward to seeing how the game evolves!

After spending around 60 hours in Where Winds Meet, I can confidently say it’s one of the most engaging new releases I’ve played in a while. The world is vibrant, full of life, and constantly pulling you toward something fun or surprising. Whether you’re exploring, fighting, crafting, or just wandering into trouble, there’s always something to keep you busy.

One of the standout features is the character design. The customization options are incredibly detailed and expansive, giving you the freedom to shape a character that genuinely feels like your own. The clothing and appearance choices are beautifully crafted, offering a huge range of styles—elegant, rugged, traditional, or flashy—so creating your perfect character never feels limiting. It’s clear a lot of care went into the designs, and it pays off every time you step into the world.

The main story is decent—good enough to keep you moving forward—but it’s the side stories that really shine. Some of them have so much depth and personality that they overshadow the main plot entirely, making exploration feel genuinely rewarding.

Gameplay-wise, the experience is smooth and exciting, and the sheer amount of content makes every hour feel worthwhile. You can easily lose track of time just drifting through its world and stumbling into new adventures.

If there’s one downside, it’s the progression system tied to the early-game time locks. Players who started on day one had to wait real-time days to achieve certain breakthroughs, which added a sense of pacing and immersion. New players, however, don’t experience those waits because the system isn’t client-sided. It would feel more balanced—and more fair—if everyone had to go through the same timed progression, giving newer players that same sense of anticipation and world wandering that the early players enjoyed.

Overall, Where Winds Meet is a fun, content-packed experience with tons of heart. A few progression inconsistencies aside, it’s absolutely worth diving into.

From the very first minutes, Where Winds Meet failed to draw me in. Despite being built on Unreal Engine, the game’s artistic direction and visuals feel surprisingly bland, lacking the impact and polish you would expect from the engine.

The characters and voice acting fall flat, offering little emotional depth or personality. The young girl you meet at the beginning is, frankly, more irritating than endearing — and that’s saying something considering even Paimon from Genshin Impact manages to be annoying in a fun way.

The early gameplay segments don’t do much to raise the bar either. Combat and movement feel average at best, with nothing particularly memorable or exciting to hold onto. One positive note is the character customization system, which is fairly robust — though similar features are becoming increasingly common across comparable games.

In the end, the strongest argument in its favor is that it’s free. Without that, I doubt it would stand out enough to avoid being forgotten as yet another unremarkable title.

[b]Edit : [/b] After looking deeper into what the game actually offers (maybe I judged it too quickly), I’m even more confused to see that many of these elements are apparently praised. The game throws in a massive mix of gameplay systems, blending concepts without ever committing to a clear direction.
There’s building, MMO elements, solo/co-op action-adventure RPG mechanics, bits of realism (from what I understand, even the healing and prison systems)… and I have absolutely no idea where to place this game now. But hey — everyone has their own taste in games.

⚔️ "Where Winds Meet" Veteran's Guide: 400 Hours from the Chinese Server 🇨🇳
Author's Note: This game is genuinely excellent, but I want to provide a transparent, critical perspective for players seeking the full picture. I have nearly 400 hours on the Chinese launch server (UID: 0105284840) and have created this guide to correct common international misunderstandings.

💰 Economics & Monetization: Is it P2W?
1. The P2W Question (Answer: No)
Healing Capacity: The Season Pass offers a small, non-significant boost to healing item capacity.

The Real Limit: Your core potion carry limit (currently 7 in the Chinese server) is increased by exchanging rewards from Stronghold First Clears, an in-game activity.

2. The Cash Shop & F2P Viability (Answer: Definitely Yes)
Obtaining Free Cosmetics: You absolutely can get high-value items without spending.

Cash Prize Pools: You regularly earn free draw tickets. With 6–8 months of play, you can obtain a top-tier $500 outfit for free (I have done this).

Seasonal Prize Pools: The green currency used for these tickets is acquired through all forms of standard gameplay (exploring, gathering, quests, chests). Progressing your exploration speed is key. (I have cleared this pool's contents twice for free).

Discounting Direct Purchases: Login rewards provide 10% discount coupons. You can stack up to five of these per item, allowing you to eventually purchase any item at half price.

The Need for Whales: The developers need support! Thank you to the big spenders who purchase luxury items—you help keep the game alive for everyone.

🎧 Quality of Life & Customization
3. Voice Acting
Strong Recommendation: Use the Chinese voice-over! It has better tone, lip-sync, and no bugs.

Story is King: Do not skip the story—it has a great plot. If you plan to skip everything, you might have more fun with a direct combat game like Naraka: Bladepoint.

4. Character Creation & Appearance
Second Character: The "Create New Character" function is currently missing because the international version is running an older client. It will be unlocked soon, mirroring the Chinese server's release schedule.

Appearance Change: You receive a free "Appearance Modification Voucher" during a main story quest (about 3 hours in) that takes you under the hospital.

11. The ESC Menu
A Known Issue: The ESC menu is notoriously complicated and may not be fixed soon (Chinese players have complained for a year).

Advice: Ignore the red notification dots. Only claim your rewards right before logging off to save time.

13. Road Signs & Chat
For a clean, uninterrupted solo experience, use the settings menu to customize the visibility of road signs, chat boxes, and scrolling messages.

14. Flight Adjustment
Crucial Tip: Go to the settings menu and choose a different camera mode for flight. This completely eliminates the annoying close-up animation and greatly improves the experience.

🗺️ Gameplay & Progression Insights
5. The Level Cap (It's Protection, Not Restriction)
Misconception: The cap is not to restrict you; it's to protect you and keep the player base together.

The Problem: I could reach max level in hours by farming Mahjong. But without exploration, you won't have the required exploration-level stats and equipment to keep up.

The Reality: The cap forces you to explore the map and acquire necessary gear sets, skill books, and weapon combinations. Trust me, you'll find this restriction reasonable in a few months.

6. Exploration
Mandatory: Explore More! Do not ignore any tasks. Every aspect of the game is directly tied to your exploration progress.

10. Multiple Currency Types
Historical Context: The different map currencies (beyond the store currency) reflect the game's setting during the tumultuous transition between the Tang and Song dynasties, a period when multiple currencies coexisted.

Narrative Depth: This detail shows how common people suffer during dynastic change, often having their life savings made worthless.

📜 Story & Lore (Deep Dive)
9. Tragedy and Historical Tide (SPOILER CONTEXT)
Character Deaths: Do not leave negative reviews because a character dies. The deaths reflect the game's brutal historical context (war, famine, and despair).

The Underground Hospital Quest: This quest explains the fate of assassins sent to reclaim the "Sixteen Prefectures." The unsuccessful, disfigured facial reconstruction surgery and their hopeless 430-year wait in the dungeons profoundly conveys the powerlessness of individuals against historical tides.

12. Quest Review System
Hidden Insights: After completing certain quests, a review system is available. Read the comments! Even I, as a Chinese player, gain deeper insight into the story's historical background from the messages left by history enthusiasts.

🌐 Server & Multiplayer Status
7. Game Longevity
No Doom-Saying: The game is doing very well in China and has even received national-level recognition. You can play with confidence.

15. Multiplayer Modes
Solo Mode: Supports up to 5-player co-op. Quest progress is individual, but exploration rewards are shared within the team.

Multiplayer mode: This is a separate mode with reduced NPC counts where quests cannot be completed. It includes exclusive content like cruise ship parties.

It's astounding how great this game looks and plays for a free release; really one of the best-looking F2P titles out there with a huge open world and Sekiro-inspired combat combined with Chinese MMO flair for a truly fresh feel. The technical state at launch was rough, though, bogging the experience down: expect glitches galore, missing voice lines, crashes, and random lag spikes or stuttering. Another negative is the recycled gameplay; outside of the great multiplayer modes, you will likely find yourself doing the same quests and exploring similar designs over and over. The main story is surprisingly long for a free-to-play game-the community estimates it's 150+ hours with time-gated progress-but starts out pretty boring, with some sections dragging on. The game has tons of mechanics, like the fun gliding/flying skills to get across the map, but you will probably just fast travel everywhere by the end. Honestly, the single and online modes feel disjointed and confusing—with story progression locked to solo, with optional private co-op for bosses, while online is mostly a social hub for PvP, guilds, raids, and endgame grinding without quests or mobs in the open world. It'd be a much better choice to have a fully seamless MMORPG with integrated persistent multiplayer.

WWM - Gorgeous Wuxia Shell With No Spine
3 / 10 – Not Recommended

WWM feels less like an MMO and more like an expensive tech demo wearing an MMO costume.

Pros

Beautiful environments and lighting. The world is often screenshot tier.
Some boss fights, like Qianye, have excellent animation and staging.
The main story has emotional moments and avoids the worst bargain bin wuxia writing.
Visual fidelity and animation quality are far above a lot of older martial arts MMOs.


Cons


Mystic skills feel half implemented and poorly explained. They sit on the UI instead of being integrated into boss mechanics or real build identity.

Core systems are shallow. Exploration is just the same few encounter templates repeated hundreds of times with different icons. Once you notice the pattern, the world feels hollow.

Gear progression is bland. It is basically level breakpoints and reskinned versions of the same weapon with slightly different set bonuses. No real buildcraft, no satisfying chase.

World leveling kills any sense of power growth. Returning to early zones only to find level 5 wolves now scaled to your level feels fake and demotivating.

Movement completely undersells the wuxia fantasy. Flight is gated behind a long animation and a very short glide window. It feels stingy, not liberating.

The economy is a mess of overlapping currencies, tokens, and shops. It feels like a mobile monetization skeleton, not a coherent RPG system, and it buries simple upgrades under layers of clutter.

Huge missed opportunity on visual identity. You get flashy cloaks, but no real character auras or cultivation visuals that would sell the fantasy.

Guild missions often feel like chores instead of social content. Being told to spam a dual emote twenty times a week is not engaging design. It is padding.

Verdict:

If you want a pretty world to run through once for the story and screenshots, WWM can deliver that. If you want a deep wuxia MMO with real systems, progression, and long term replay value, it feels like a promise that never made it past the concept art stage. Not recommended in its current state.

Honestly I was a bit disappointed with this game. It sounded really exciting, a sort of Wuxia themed combination of souls-like combat, RPG elements, MMO elements, and more. For context, I'm someone who loves souls-like games, and I've read Wuxia novels since I was in middle school, so it seemed perfect for me. The skeleton of a good game is definitely present, but I think its muddled by many small issues, which when together, strip a lot of the enjoyability of the game for me. Starting with the translations, while they weren't horrible, at times they definitely felt awkward in some spots of the game, along with some very odd voice acting quality. Some of the characters had good voice acting, some had none, some had extremely obvious AI voices that sounded terrible, sometimes random lines would have no voiceover, while later lines in the same dialogue would have a voiceover. It just feels very messy and rushed. On the topic of AI, some of the NPC's in this game are AI powered, meaning they have AI voiceovers, and you can chat to an AI chatbot acting like the character. Its an interesting idea, but I think the execution in the end is pretty poor. The AI has no integration with the game environment besides attacking you if you're too rude to them, so it can be pretty immersion breaking when they mention taking certain actions which they can't actually do in game. It just ends up feeling lazy to me, like they couldn't be bothered to create dialogue for some of the less important characters around the world or actually voice act them out. Moving on, the menus are quite convoluted in this game. After a while you can mostly understand what to do, but it certainly doesn't make it easy to enjoy the game, with many UI elements and stats having next to no explanation of what they actually do. I think the last straw for me was some of the minigames around the map. For example, Gift of Gab is genuinely one of the most awful things I've seen in a game. It's a debate minigame where you get inspiration, and can then use that inspiration to play cards that "do damage" to the opponents psyche, while they do the same. Each one of the cards do different things, and there are some more mechanics that I won't go in detail about. It sounds nice on the surface, but during the tutorial for it, the game just starts playing in the background, so you can't really read anything, and honestly, you can't even read anything anyway. The game moves so quickly you genuinely cannot even read the cards. Most people I've seen just button mash, spamming cards until they win or lose. Its actually braindead design. In the end, the game just comes off as sloppy to me, which is a shame, because the core aspects of the game are quite good. The combat feels nice, the world is fun to explore, and there are some cool bosses, but ultimately I think whether you'll like this game or not comes down to how much of the small flaws you can tolerate.

[h1]Preface[/h1]
First off, the game itself if you know that it's a gacha and enjoy those kinds of games, is very good. The reviews of 84% positive as of writing is deserved and I wish I could be moving this number up as well. However, there is one part of it which I genuinely feel should be corrected before I do so.

[h1]The Review[/h1]
I'm gonna split this into two sections. First the positives, and then ending with a negative. I know I've only played for 2 hours, but it's 2 hours which let me see the first intro boss, get into the "home" village, and then a tiny little bit after that. I will play more of this and maybe update some of the review if I feel like there needs to be changes that reflect my new experience. Additionally, if they rectify and correct the negative portion, then I will change it to a positive review. Now, let's start with the main review.

[h3]Positives[/h3]
So I'm not gonna cover too many points, mainly because I haven't played it enough yet. But there are some first impressions I genuinely want to point out.

[b]Controller Support[/b]
This should come at no surprise. I've played some of NetEase's other games they've published, and generally since their games are also mobile first, their controller support is always top notch. If you come from Dark Souls, Sekiro, or particularly Elden Ring, while there are some differences, the general experience should just click for you immediately and straight up get you going. They really nailed this part of the game.

[b]Performance[/b]
A bit surprised about this one honestly. I didn't tweak any settings going into this, and playing on a 180Hz 1440p monitor with an RTX 4070, Ryzen 9 9950X3D and 96GB 6000MHz CL32, a lot of other bigger games recently has run at dramatically lower FPS than I would have expected in a just previous gen GPU. While I only really reach half of the refresh-rate, I do still get the frames at a stable rate with little to no stutters. And this is while the game has defaulted to everything on max settings, with any form of upscaling turned off completely. (I know my setup is hella scuffed too with the CPU + GPU combo that I have, but it shouldn't change the review in any way). 

[b]Combat & Story[/b]
I'm putting this in the same category because I have similar experiences with both, even if they generally should be split. I just wouldn't need to write the same thing twice this way. Both the Combat and Story feels better than I expected. Coming from both Genshin Impact and Zenless Zone Zero, but particularly the former, I feel that Where Winds Meet's story make sense in a way that is different than the other two games in a very positive way. With the combat in Genshin Impact, I often found myself repeatedly dashing through enemies when attacking normally, which doesn't happen here, and Story wise, the story in Genshin Impact felt very "forced" and "complex". I'm sure this could change with Where Winds Meet when I keep playing, but so far for my first impressions, the intro sequence at least make sense and I feel it could realistically happen. At least compared to the other two games I've played as I mentioned.

[h3]Negatives[/h3]
There was two points I wanted to cover here, but I had a false impression of one of them which was the Crime/Wanted system. I looked up how they work, and have since removed it from the review because it actually makes sense and could actually be quite interesting. The latter one is however still my main point for giving it a negative review (which shouldn't come at a surprise given it violates steam's developer agreement) so I'm still keeping it in until they do something about it.

[b]Undisclosed use of Generative-AI[/b]
In January of 2024 Valve put out [url=https://store.steampowered.com/news/group/4145017/view/3862463747997849618]this blog post about "AI Content on Steam"[/url]. In it, there's two points that need to be mentioned in the Content Survey, and this would then show up for the users wanting to play, in the same area you usually see the use of third party EULAs or Kernel level anti cheat.

The two points in the blog post first mentions [u]Pre-Generated Gen-AI content[/u]. This would include things like voice lines bundled with the game which uses Text To Speech or textures which uses Text To Image, which is then bundled with the game when it's released. The game uses this for some NPCs.
  These NPCs also have a chat feature where you can quite obviously talk to an LLM (Large Language Model) and have an active conversation where it understands the context and what you say. This would fall under the second point the blog post mentions, namely [u]Live-Generated Gen-AI content[/u]. This is because the content is generated on-the-fly while you're playing the game, just as you're typing messages to the NPC.

Neither of these two are disclosed on the store page where they should be.

[h1]Summary[/h1]
I personally don't mind the use of Gen-AI. If you have the rights to everything you've used to train the model, Gen-AI can actually be quite useful. Assuming this is the case, I want to recommend this game because the overall experience has been quite positive. But until they disclose this use of Gen-AI to the users as per the steam developer and publishing agreement, I cannot recommend this game.

Where Winds Meet is genuinely a phenomenal game. The combat feels sharp, fluid, and responsive, and the open world is absolutely gorgeous—easily one of the most visually striking settings I’ve stepped into recently. Even the early quests feel engaging, and I’m curious to see how much deeper they get as the story unfolds.

That said, there’s one thing that really soured my initial experience: the lack of shared progression in co-op. For me, that’s a crucial feature. I want to group up with friends, run quests, explore the world, and have everyone’s progress count—no matter who’s hosting the session.

Right now, if you’re not the host, the quests you do together barely matter for your own story. It feels punishing, especially when you look at how seamlessly games like Destiny or World of Warcraft handle shared progression. I really hope that as development continues, the game adopts a more fluid, unified progression system so co-op feels rewarding for everyone involved.

Aside from that issue, the game is amazing. If shared progression isn’t a dealbreaker for you, Where Winds Meet is absolutely worth playing.

And finally, the amount of reward schemes and progression tracks you have to go into an obscure segment of the menu to claim is truly ridiculous. I played for barely 3 hours and I felt like I had to stop every 15 seconds just to click away a marker indicating I've earned an award. Maybe it slows down later on, but that is not a newbie friendly system.

Overall the game feels purposefully designed to appeal to brainless checklist completioning, it has the look and feel of an MMO even though you can play entirely solo. But therein lies the problem; Classical MMO models are just objectively bad.

I don't want to hate on this game, it offers a ton of content and is extraordinarily well polished while not [i]technically[/i] costing you a damn thing. But underneath that too-good-to-be-true layer lies a predatory whale-catching system that is almost as sinister as Diablo IV.

You can argue that it's all optional and therefore no one is harming anyone but themselves by buying into it. But that's true of real life gambling too, nobody [i]has[/i] to go to a casino, but we all know they still do. It is no longer a valid excuse to leave the responsibility entirely on the consumer.

If this game had simply cost €70 and had no in-game transactions of any kind, I would've happily paid that and played this game to completion.

Where Winds Meet could have been something, but almost every part of it feels designed to waste your time. The story and side quests are mind numbing. The most important settings are hidden behind 7~8 pages of interfaces and I have to really look where I need to click to find it, and the help function is useless, it doesn't let you type more than a handful of characters in, probably because it's made with Chinese character limits in mind. The inventory section is poorly sorted and the icons are hard to decipher, and a lot of the things I've collected either serve no purpose or doesn't have a clear purpose, clogging up inventory and making it hard to read. I don't know. There are three main classes namely tank, DPS, healer, but the definition of the classes in this game is extremely blurry or nonexistent because anyone can be a healer and do an absurdly high amount of damage and take a lot of damage, it does not reward you and make you feel that you're getting better at any role, in fact it gets more punishing as the enemy balance continues to worsen the more bosses you encounter. If I have to search the Internet for "how-to" videos / wiki articles just to manage the basics, this is an entirely fundamental problem in this game. Even if I had the privilege to understand Chinese, I looked up multiple sites to find what I need help with, but there are either no guides, or anything relevant to this game's topic, even though this game has been out for more than a year at this point.

It feels the developers were so busy pouring in all of these "cool" features that they overlooked providing information to players about how to use / manage those features. And there are endless screens of stuff - constantly presented with new screens. Impossible to keep track of so much data.

The game feigns complexity by adding a bunch of jargon and word salad, even hard for a Chinese to understand. - it's just frustrating when there doesn't appear to be any path to understanding the complexity. 可以说，我已经给了这个游戏很多的机会，我用了不到60~70个小时就通关了。我真的很想想喜欢这款游戏。它画面很美，但缺点实在太多了。

这款游戏的文档实在太差劲了，即使像我这样的中国人也难以理解。我在游戏和现实生活中都遇到过很多令人困惑的界面，但这款游戏绝对是其中最混乱的一个。最重要的设置竟然藏在七八页的界面后面，我必须仔细查找才能找到，而且帮助功能也形同虚设，输入的字数限制非常严格，可能是因为它是按照中文的字数限制设计的。物品栏的分类也很混乱，图标难以辨认，很多我收集到的东西要么毫无用处，或者用途不明，堆满了物品栏，很难阅读。我真是无语了。游戏里有三大职业：坦克、输出和治疗。但这些职业的定义极其模糊，甚至可以说是不存在的，因为任何人都可以治疗，而且输出伤害高得离谱，也能够承受很多伤害，一个火车砸下去都不会死的那种。这种设计既不会让你觉得自己在任何角色上有所进步，反而会随着遇到越多的怪平衡越来越差，觉得自己在游戏里没什么成长。如果我需要上网搜索教程视频/维基百科才能掌握基本操作，这绝对是游戏的一个根本性问题。即使我懂中文，我也查了很多网站，但要么找不到攻略，要么找不到任何与游戏相关的资料，而这款游戏已经上线一年多了。

感觉开发者们忙着堆砌各种炫酷的功能，却忽略了向玩家提供如何使用/管理这些功能的信息。而且游戏里充斥着无穷无尽的界面——新的界面层出不穷。根本无法追踪如此庞大的数据量。

这款游戏试图通过堆砌大量术语和晦涩难懂的文字来营造复杂性，就连中国人也难以理解。最令人沮丧的是，玩家似乎找不到任何理解这种复杂性的方法。此外，疾病系统也没有意思，只是用一堆术语吓唬玩家，玩家只需要去诊所或让其他玩家帮忙治疗即可。这个系统尤其缺乏深度。

我玩游戏的理由很明确：要么游戏性好，要么剧情好。而这款游戏在这两方面都表现不佳。大家都知道这款游戏漏洞百出，我就不赘述了。然而，剧情嘛……没什么好说的，因为它实在乏味，没有一个角色值得让人产生感情或印象深刻，因为他们都像NPC一样，而且每个人的哲学和缘由都愚蠢至极，包括游戏的主角在内。

我不是一遇到什么就退坑的人，但如果游戏之后继续让我失望，而且没有任何改进，我会立刻弃坑。

Where Winds Meet has great potential, but, sadly, its atrocious localization ruins the experience — and that alone is enough to make me drop the game.

Still, let's start with the positives:
- WWM is gorgeous. I was drawn in by the Chinese aesthetics and wasn’t disappointed. Honestly, just walking around to enjoy the scenery and architecture is a good enough reason to download it.
- Performance is quite solid for the picture you get.
- The combat system is pretty fun and fluid, with a wide variety of weapons and skills to experiment with.
- It’s free, and the monetization is cosmetics-only.

Now for the glaring issue. Most of the English translation was done by AI, and it seems no one bothered to edit any of it. I don’t care much about the voice acting, since you can just switch to Chinese, which is handled fairly well. But if I’m playing a large, story-driven game set in a foreign country, with tons of dialogue and lore, the text has to be of decent quality. Right now, it’s nowhere close. To make matters worse, subtitles are not properly formatted and often poorly synchronized, giving you about a second to read two lines of text. With English not being my native language, you can imagine how frustrating all that becomes.

Some minor issues:
- Progression and menus are convoluted. There’s just way too much unnecessary stuff.
- Even with upscalers turned off, there’s ghosting around the character whenever the camera moves.
- Ubisoft-esque open world activities and collectibles, many of which feel shallow.
- The NPC AI-chatbot system is extremely primitive. Even if you try to roleplay and take it seriously, it breaks too easily.

I’d be happy to give WWM another shot, but only after major improvements to the localization.

Game itself is good.
World feels alive, NPCs feel human, battle system is okay, many interesting activities. I give credit, where credit is due. this could had been a positive review if not for the part that everyone seems to be afraid to talk about - business model.

I wish to make two things very clear:
Firstly, NO service provider is entitled to understanding of intricacies of their business or any sort of good will. Good will (and wish to repay or buy services) is at sole disgression of consumer based on value provided. In other words argument "game dev wants to eat" does not work if said dev is asking for too much for too little and I (or anyone else for the matter) have no obligation to care how many people work at their company and how high salaries they need to keep their things running.

Secondly, I am aware, that this game is NOT P2W in a strict sense of a word. When people say that "Game is not P2W" as an argument to defend this game's business model, I consider it a bad faith argument, since it is made on a false assumption, that microtransaction based model can be evil or unfair when and only when game becomes unplayable without utilizing paid options. Knowing video game player psychology, it is plain obvious that player wants to look good and/or express himself no less than he wants to see big numbers in his stat sheet. Therefore the distinction between monetizing good looks or stats is superficial.

Any Gamedev studio needs to make money to function, it is understandable. True question is how much money is it fair to demand in return for the value they offer and how the offer is made?

In-game purchases in this game start from 1$ and go beyond 50$.
and then, this game utilizes the full arsenal of marketing practices: convoluted system of multiple currencies to 
 obfuscate the true price of a lot of items, limited time offers, battlepass etc. And then we get to a heavy emphasis on social interaction to increase pressure on potential buyers to spend more. It does not quite matter if lower bar for in-game purchases is 1$ if anyone and their horse will have the cheap stuff and good old "oh, that guy/gal has that hair, I want too" or "my neighbor made his character look in a certain way, I must make mine look even better" sentiments kick in. Stakes will inevitably be raised.

I can imagine, there could be people in this world, for whom anything below 1000$ is a pocket change, but for an average person (a teacher, firefighter, man from the factory etc) in Japan, US or gods forbid, places like Indochina or East Europe 40-50$ is significant spending for one little nothing in a video game (especially considering you very likely can't keep it in any shape or form when one day in future the game dies and servers will have to be shut off). But it will not be just 50$ for an item. It will be hair from one purchase, dress from other and horse from third.

To sum it up, business model of this game is far from innocent and comes as dangerously close to what happens in gambling as possible even if it is not P2W. 40-50$ is a fair price for a full game, not for a little dress or a hairstyle in the game. In a healthy society, a person who claims otherwise should be perceived as speaking utter and complete nonsense.

I can appreciate the suprisingly decent exploration and the sheer number of minigames with online interactions, I can excuse the typical 'mobile game' feature stank these types of game usually suffer from, but I'm deeply disappointed on how this game handles the arguably most important thing - combat. I've defeated multiple major bosses and a world boss solo on expert and if you're expecting soulsike gameplay - the comparisons to sekiro are definitely less than honest, as this game is more like Nioh and less like Souls. What I'm about to say will sound like common Fromsoftware shilling but these types of games have either really good and polished combat, or they fall flat in the deep ocean of mediocrity which is unfortunately the case both with Nioh (imo) and this game. Mobility is fast yet clunky, as the character usually takes a long time to react to inputs. Enemies are damage sponges which prolongs the fights unnecesarilly. Visual clarity is quite bad with tons of flashy effects spinning around you and your targets. Missing deflects on any part of a combo is severely punishing which is unfair at best, considering no proper alternative for defence in this game (blocking and dodging are definitely not meant to be used as a replacement for deflects). Feels like bosses have a lot of true combos (true, as in 'miss 1 deflect and watch your character get hit by the whole combo' feeling). Some hitboxes tied to some animations are questionable at best. 

All in all I played this game hoping to get a fun, funfilling combat. As many such cases, the game tries to copy Souls but fails to offer comparable level of polishness and things that 'just make sense' in terms of combat fluidity, fairness and challenge.

You might like it if you don't care or have more tolerance to wannabe soulslike experiences, especially since other features are genuinely interesting despite f2p-mobile-gacha aura this game reeks of. The most important thing for me turned out to be mediocre, so all these mechanics around combat lead to annoyance and frustration.

I really want to love this game, and there is a lot in it I do love. There's lots to explore, the art and animation is great. Everything is surface level fantastic. But mechanically the combat is just untuned. Playing on legend difficulty, so ymmv with these points as I don't know how the lower difficulty experience feels with assisted parries.

- Timing for parries is way early and really short. Because you can not time it with when the attack is actually hitting your hitbox, you have to guess at when the moment is somewhere before the swing is actually going to hit you, but not where you would naturally parry in say Sekiro, or Ghost of Tsushima. Its super awkward and instead of it getting you into a rhythm it makes you guess constantly. Which leads into the second point;
- Many enemy attacks either hover FOREVER, or come out INSTANTLY - there is very few times that are in between and most attacks have perfect tracking (mid air turntables included) and insane 2 frame gap close. 
- the enemy damage scaling is insane. like forget bosses, trash mobs 2-3 shots you even at level cap because the game scales up every trash mob faster than you gain power, so you are always fighting a losing battle and never actually get to feel powerful against anyone or anything.
- Even blocking you take obscene damage amd block is a different button to parry, so you find yourself having to tie up a keypress on block constantly because the parry is so inconsistently timed between boss attacks. On top of this, blocking also eats chunks out of whatever they call your stagger bar. It needs to pick a lane.
- There is a reason bloodborne is the only fromsoft game that had you farm for healing pots. It is bad. Having to run around for ages farming mats, or alternatively dumping a mountain of coins on buying them meant I had to do most bosses without healing to conserve resources unless I was close to victory.
- You will spend most of your time in game with access to only 2-3 pots for a fight at most because the collect-a-thon for improving your pot supply on hand is frankly, kinda obscene.

Is it impossible? No, I've certainly level capped and beaten a few bosses a bunch of times in solo and often underleveled. But I never once came away from a fight thinking it was fun or fair; even on the genuinely cool looking bosses with neat ideas behind them. It was always thank fuck that absolute bullshit is over, and until that mechanically changes, I just can not recommend this game.

Where Winds Meet is a boring game.

Don't misunderstand, the game is beautiful and the gameplay is well choreographed.  However, it tries to be Dark Souls and ends up being Wo Long.  Gear is a pointless numbers-go-up grind and character development is simply a matter of higher levels giving you access to gear with bigger numbers.  All the depth and personality the Souls games allow through weapon selection, spell selection, and stat adjustment are simply lacking in Where Winds Meet.

What we're left with is a boring, one-note experience where combat relies first and foremost on a player's ability to memorize enemy attack strings and parry them perfectly to deplete their Qi bar and open them up to execution attacks.  A few of these execution attacks and the fight is over, and the piddling chip damage you do through your own attacks along the way doesn't amount to a shorter fight.  It's an infuriatingly reactive system and ultimately led me to quit the game with half the time still left on my battle pass because I was sick of standing there mashing parry until I was allowed to win.

Complain complain: Getting into the details of gameplay, the UI is as intuitive as building a nuclear reactor from potato chips. It feels like a game made by people that all have ADHD or a development studio so large they just gave each of the 100 people working free range to create a mini-game or some crap. Beyond an insane number of activities, most have some kind of stupid currency attached. Some of the mini-games are fun, but they are hard to find in the open world (ex debates and healing). They try to cover this with a MMO element, forcing you to take bounties from other players. The issue being you can NEVER get ones related to jobs unless you have bots working for you - they get snatched up that quick. The martial arts, which you would think is center stage in this type of game, are few and not as exciting to unlock because they are just 1-button skills rather than a revamp of a fighting style. The combat feels like Dark Souls even on story mode, where stamina always seems to run out in a boss fight and every boss seems to replenish its health 2-3 times for no reason. [hr][/hr]
[h2]1. DEI Injected.[/h2]
For the western release of this game, Genders (Male / Female) has been removed and replaced with "Body types". [url=https://steamcommunity.com/groups/Slistingservice/discussions/0/4307201374342406741/]Read why that is bad here.[/url]

[hr][/hr]
[h2]2. User Interface.[/h2]
Oh dear god the UI. Layers inside other layers that are inside other layers.. A map that is borderline completely unusable because if you are not almost FULLY zoomed in, icons and POI's disappear and then there's the 10+ different pages to collect "rewards". Waypoint markers? Yeah those are still in Chinese. You have to experience it for yourself to understand just how bad it is.

[hr][/hr]

It basically doesn't exist. Same, if not worse draconic restrictions than on Dark Souls. 90% of the content is Single-Player only.

[hr][/hr]
[h2]4. AI Generated Content.[/h2]
Undisclosed on the store page for some reason. It's used when creating character faces, voices and generating dialogue for NPC chatting in the game. Most if not all of the English voices are AI generated as well. There's dozens of times (especially later) where they literally bug out.

[hr][/hr]
[h2]5. Fake Progression.[/h2]
The devs unfortunately decided to implement the bane of all RPG's: "Level Scaling" into this game. Meaning, mobs and bosses scale to your level constantly, making the whole "leveling up" and "getting gear" aspect of this game completely pointless and a 100% artificial grind. When i started out, i fought a bear. Learning combat, i took 5+ hits but ultimately won. Came back to the area much later as a higher level with new, fully upgraded gear, fought the same bear and he killed me in 2 shots.

Want to dive towards something in your talents? Sorry, that's level locked. Want to explore the world or go get upgrades important to your build outside of the starting area? Nope, progression AND strictly time-locked, get teleported back dummy. All the "content" in the world? It's 5000x copy-pasted garbage served on a Ubisoft style plate but with even more pointless minigames. Won a hard battle and excited to get better gear? Sorry but all the loot in the world is pretty much just money and gear upgrade currencies. You get all the gear at once for free whenever you "breakthrough" (remove your level cap with a small trial.. Why is there a level cap? I don't know.)

[hr][/hr]
[h2]6. Boss Designs.[/h2]
A few are good (hard but fair), an overwhelming majority are not. Imagine fighting through a tough boss, having mastered all of their moves. You get through the first stage without taking a hit. Then the second stage starts. You get him down to 25% hp and then oops, you slipped up for 0.1 seconds and now you're dead in a insta-kill combo regardless of gear. Back to the first stage! [b]Yup,[/b] that kind of design becomes the norm after the opening and it's pretty clear they've been added in as a panicked afterthought in response to people beating them too easily. All the boss arenas are also really claustrophobic, including ones with invisible borders such as with Qianye and i don't know why. 

For those that have played Elden Ring, most bosses unfortunately suffer from a mixture of Godrick and Pontiff syndrome. [b]AKA:[/b] Attacks are artificially staggered, delayed with tons of "oh i'm holding my weapon up here but am i going to swing it?... wait for it.." and Pontiff's 5+ second long combos that you pretty much just have to sit there and wait through. Obnoxious, artificially difficult (learning moves > reactive gameplay) and ultimately incredibly unfun. They also just throw you into bosses at the beginning without letting you do any settings or choose your weapon which is.. A strange choice. Devs seem very confused in general.

[hr][/hr]
[h2]7. Combat.[/h2]
On the surface, it's quite solid and definitely stands out. Unfortunately, due to all the enemy designs being what they are, the core of it boils down to having the same crippling problems that Sekiro had which is a 95% emphasis being placed upon parrying. 100% damage negation + you stun them (including bosses), can be used on pretty much all attacks, including AoE's? That is going to dictate the entire game's design.

Once combined with the previously mentioned Godrick syndrome on most enemies, combat boils down to learning patterns above all else. You can negate SOME of this as the game lets you bring two weapon types and due to the sheer length of boss fights (+ you finite amount of healing items that needs to be grinded + crafted, yes really), people pretty much always opt to bringing the self-healing fans but ultimately, you're just drowning slightly slower if you don't parry (deflect).

If you're fighting regular human-sized opponents or smaller, you get no warnings for their attacks and can't realistically see them coming at all if you're hitting them due to flashy effects that can't be turned off, especially if it's dark. The camera is also quite awful, being extremely close to the point where you're 100% blind to enemies behind you and has some clunky mouse smoothing thing going on which can't be turned off.

[hr][/hr]
[h2]8. Bugs.[/h2]
There's a bunch. I got soft-locked about 4-5 times up to level 25, having to restart the game because of a mix of getting stuck inside solid terrain (there's no unstuck feature, open a chest at the wrong angle and you're screwed), quest objectives not spawning or letting you interact with them, mobs not dying even if you throw them off 500 foot cliffs, etc. This game was NOT ready for release.

The scaling is also clearly completely broken & all over the place, both for bosses that can go from being easy to complete mountain HP sponges depending on your level and for certain mobs, like the Aureate Pavilion that can 1-2 shot you (depending on level) with their fire throwing combos and appear in groups of 5+.
